newsitem.title: USA: Clinton stresses education in State of Union talk.
newsitem.headline: Clinton stresses education in State of Union talk.

text.p: In a State of the Union speech setting his second-term goals, President Bill Clinton said on Tuesday night that improving U.S. education would get top priority followed by "unfinished business" like campaign finance reform.

The televised address before the joint houses of Congress, appeared to be a compilation of poll-tested themes from his 1996 re-election campaign and represented what a senior aide called a "concrete plan of action" for preparing America for the 21st century.

In excerpts from the speech released ahead of the 9 p.m. EST (0200 GMT Wednesday) speech, Clinton appealed for a "national crusade" to raise education standards to a level competitive with other industrial nations.

"The greatest step of all -- the high threshold to the future we now must cross -- and my number one priority as president for the next four years -- is to ensure that Americans have the best education in the world," he said in his prepared text.

"We must begin a national crusade for education standards -- not federal government standards, but national standards representing what all of our students must know to succeed in the knowledge economy of the 21st Century."
He proposed $51 billion for education in the fiscal year starting Oct. 1, a 20 percent increase over current spending, to pay for education, training and tax cuts tied to education.
Under his education programme spending would rise to nearly $60 billion a year by 2002 even as other programmes are cut to balance the federal budget by that year.

Clinton went into the annual ritual in the chamber of the House of Representatives, with a television audience of millions, enjoying some of the highest public approval ratings of his presidency -- 63 percent -- in spite of a nagging controversy over how he and his Democratic Party raised money for last year's campaigns.

Trying to take the sting out of that issue and put pressure on the Republican-controlled Congress, he appealed anew for campaign finance reform -- and set a specific date of July 4, the Independence Day holiday, for completing the work.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, was cautious on Clinton's challenge, saying it should first be determined what laws were violated last year. A team of FBI agents is investigating and congressional oversight hearings are planned.
"I don't see how you can decide what you need to do in terms of reform until you see how existing laws are being violated or abused," Lott told reporters.
Clinton's speech, expected to last about an hour, was thin on grand, large-scale initiatives -- in line with the country's perceived mood toward less government intrusion.

But he was clearly hoping to make education his ticket to the history books, in addition to two big items left over from his first term: balancing the budget by 2002 and carrying out a welfare reform law signed last year in a way that gets people jobs.
He was to lay out specifics of his proposals in his budget blueprint for fiscal 1998 to be unveiled Thursday.
In a appeal for racial harmony, Clinton noted that he had taken the oath of office with his hand on a Bible open to a passage from the prophet Isaiah urging reconciliation.

"I placed my hand on that verse when I took the oath of office, on behalf of all Americans. For no matter what our differences -- in our faiths, our backgrounds, our politics -- we must all be repairers of the breach. We may not share a common past, but surely we have a common future," he said.
The pastor who suggested the Isaiah quote, television evangelist Robert Schuller, was seated with Clinton's wife Hillary during the speech.

Clinton's national education crusade involves a 10-point plan, topped by setting up a programme in the next two years for national achievement tests in 4th grade reading and 8th grade math to make sure children master the basics. He would increase student access to the Internet.

The crusade would also include ensuring high quality standards for teachers, make sure students can read on their own by the end of the 3rd grade, make schools safe, disciplined and drug-free, and modernise schools.
